A rule without `match` is general and is never highlighted. `mark` (optional) is the stressed syllable, shown in bold. British English (modern Standard Southern British), US notes where useful. Rule ids are the old slot ids (content-plan §1.3). Not yet reviewed by a teacher.

rules.title: Word stress
rules.text: Every English word with two or more syllables has one strong syllable. Most nouns and adjectives with two syllables are strong at the start. Many verbs with two syllables are strong at the end. Words that end in -tion or -sion are strong just before the ending. The other syllables are short and weak.

rules.title: Short i or long ee
rules.text: The vowel in ship /ɪ/ is short and relaxed. The vowel in sheep /iː/ is long, and your lips are spread, as in a smile. ee is always long. ea is usually long, but a few common words have a short e /e/: bread, head, weather.

rules.title: The weak vowel /ə/
rules.text: /ə/ is the most common sound in English: a short, quiet “uh”. Weak syllables often have it, whatever the spelling. Small words like a, to, of, and, for are weak in a sentence too: a cup of tea = /ə kʌp əv tiː/.

rules.title: Vowel + consonant + e
rules.text: When a word ends in vowel + consonant + e, the e is silent and the vowel says its letter name: hat → hate, kit → kite, hop → hope, cut → cute. Some very common words don't follow this rule: have, give, live, come, love, some.

rules.title: th: /θ/ and /ð/
rules.text: Put the tip of your tongue between your teeth and push air out. In think and three, it is only air /θ/. In this, the and mother, you use your voice too /ð/. It is not s, t, f, z or d: think ≠ sink, three ≠ tree.

rules.title: -ed: /t/, /d/ or /ɪd/
rules.text: The past ending -ed has three sounds. After p, k, s, sh, ch, f, x it is /t/: helped, watched. After other sounds it is /d/: played, lived. Only after t and d is it a new syllable /ɪd/: wanted, needed.

rules.title: sp, st, sk at the start
rules.text: Many English words start with two or three consonants: sp, st, sk, sm, sn, sl, str, spr. Say them together. Don't put a vowel before them: school, not “eschool”, and street, not “istreet”.

rules.title: -s: /s/, /z/ or /ɪz/
rules.text: Plurals (cats) and verbs after he, she, it (he works) end in -s. After p, t, k, f it is /s/: cats, books. After other sounds it is /z/: dogs, plays. After s, z, sh, ch, ge it is a new syllable /ɪz/: buses, watches, oranges.

rules.title: b, d, g, v, z at the end
rules.text: At the end of an English word, b, d, g, v and z keep their voice. Don't change them to p, t, k, f, s: bad ≠ bat, bag ≠ back, prize ≠ price. The vowel before them is also a little longer.

rules.title: r: only before a vowel
rules.text: In British English you say r only before a vowel sound: red, very, sorry. After a vowel, r is silent and the vowel is often long: car /kɑː/, card /kɑːd/, teacher /ˈtiːtʃə/. When the next word starts with a vowel, the r comes back: far away. US English says every r.

rules.title: h
rules.text: h at the start of a word is a soft breath, like breathing on a cold window: house, happy. Don't leave it out (hear ≠ ear) and don't make it hard in the throat. A few words have a silent h: hour, honest, honour. So we say an hour.

rules.title: w and v
rules.text: For w, make your lips small and round, as for “oo”, then open them: we, water, what. Your teeth don't touch your lips. For v, put your top teeth on your bottom lip and use your voice: very, van. wine and vine are two different words.

rules.title: Silent letters
rules.text: Some letters are written but not said. k before n at the start: know, knife. w before r: write, wrong. b after m at the end: climb, comb. l in walk, talk, half. gh in night, light, daughter.

rules.title: Linking words
rules.text: In normal speech, English joins a word that ends in a consonant to a next word that starts with a vowel. There is no stop between them: an apple sounds like “a napple”, get up like “ge tup”.
